questions.question: The modern sandwich is named after which English aristocrat?
questions.fun_fact: John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich, allegedly asked for meat between two slices of bread in 1762 so he could keep playing cards without greasy fingers.

questions.question: Which country is widely credited with inventing the croissant?
questions.fun_fact: The croissant descends from the Austrian 'kipferl'. It only became 'French' after Viennese baker August Zang opened a bakery in Paris in 1839.

questions.question: Which two countries officially dispute the invention of French fries?
questions.fun_fact: Belgians claim fries were invented in the Meuse Valley in the 1600s. The 'French' label likely comes from US soldiers in WWI who heard French-speaking Belgians.

questions.question: Hawaiian pizza was actually invented in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Greek-Canadian Sam Panopoulos invented Hawaiian pizza in Chatham, Ontario in 1962. The name comes from the brand of canned pineapple he used.

questions.question: General Tso's chicken, a staple of American Chinese menus, originated in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Chef Peng Chang-kuei created it in Taiwan in the 1950s. It was sweetened and battered for American tastes when it reached New York in the 1970s.

questions.question: Tikka masala, often called Britain's national dish, was likely invented in which city?
questions.fun_fact: The dish is widely attributed to Glasgow chef Ali Ahmed Aslam in the 1970s, who reportedly added tomato soup and cream to a customer's 'too dry' chicken tikka.

questions.question: Although associated with Chinese restaurants in the West, fortune cookies actually originated in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Fortune cookies trace back to 19th-century Japanese 'tsujiura senbei'. They became associated with Chinese restaurants in California in the early 1900s.

questions.question: Vindaloo, a famously fiery Indian curry, has its name rooted in which European language?
questions.fun_fact: Vindaloo comes from the Portuguese 'carne de vinha d'alhos' (meat in wine and garlic), brought to Goa by Portuguese colonisers.

questions.question: Spaghetti Bolognese, as served abroad, is barely recognised in which Italian city?
questions.fun_fact: In Bologna, ragù is traditionally served with tagliatelle, not spaghetti. The mayor once asked foreign restaurants to stop calling it 'spaghetti bolognese'.

questions.question: The chimichanga, a deep-fried burrito, was reportedly invented in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Legend credits Monica Flin of El Charro Café in Tucson, Arizona (1922), who accidentally dropped a burrito into a deep fryer and exclaimed a Spanish swear word she cleaned up to 'chimichanga'.

questions.question: Which active ingredient was originally in Coca-Cola in the late 1800s?
questions.fun_fact: Coca-Cola contained small amounts of cocaine from coca leaf extract until around 1903. Today it still uses 'decocainised' coca leaf extract for flavour.

questions.question: Under EU law, sparkling wine can only be called 'Champagne' if it comes from which region?
questions.fun_fact: The protected designation of origin restricts the name 'Champagne' to sparkling wine produced in the Champagne region using specific grape varieties and methods.

questions.question: Kopi luwak coffee is famous (and expensive) because the beans are first processed by what?
questions.fun_fact: Asian palm civets eat the coffee cherries, and the beans are collected from their droppings. Enzymes in their gut alter the beans' flavour.

questions.question: Pu-erh tea is unusual because it is intentionally what?
questions.fun_fact: Pu-erh from Yunnan, China, is microbially fermented and can age for decades. Vintage cakes can sell for thousands of dollars per kilogram.

questions.question: Real absinthe gets its green colour primarily from what?
questions.fun_fact: Traditional absinthe's green hue comes from chlorophyll in the final steeping with herbs like hyssop and petite wormwood. The colour naturally fades to amber over time.

questions.question: Gin gets its dominant flavour from which botanical?
questions.fun_fact: By legal definition in the EU and US, a spirit cannot be called gin unless juniper is the predominant flavour.

questions.question: Tequila can only legally be called tequila if it's made from which plant?
questions.fun_fact: Tequila must be made from at least 51% Blue Weber agave and produced in specific regions of Mexico, primarily Jalisco.

questions.question: Butter tea, a staple in Tibet, is typically made with butter from which animal?
questions.fun_fact: Tibetan po cha mixes tea with yak butter and salt. It's drunk all day to combat dehydration and chapped lips at high altitudes.

questions.question: Root beer originally got its distinctive flavour from the root of which plant, later banned by the FDA?
questions.fun_fact: Sassafras root contains safrole, a compound the FDA banned as a food additive in 1960 over cancer concerns. Modern root beer uses safrole-free flavourings.

questions.question: The Maillard reaction, responsible for browning seared meat and toast, is a reaction between what?
questions.fun_fact: Named after French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard, it's distinct from caramelisation (which is only sugars) and creates hundreds of flavour compounds.

questions.question: Why does garlic sometimes turn blue or green when pickled or cooked with acid?

answers.text: Sulphur compounds react with amino acids
It absorbs copper from the pot

questions.fun_fact: Garlic's allicin reacts with amino acids to form harmless pigments called pyrroles. The garlic is still safe to eat.

questions.question: 'Sous vide' literally translates from French as what?
questions.fun_fact: Food is sealed in a vacuum bag and cooked in a precisely controlled water bath, allowing very even, consistent cooking impossible with traditional methods.

questions.question: The cooking term 'al dente' literally means what in Italian?
questions.fun_fact: It describes pasta cooked so it still has a slight firmness when bitten — a texture preferred for both flavour and a lower glycaemic response.

questions.question: Adding salt to water for boiling raises the boiling point by roughly how much for normal cooking amounts?
questions.fun_fact: You'd need to dissolve enormous amounts of salt to meaningfully raise the boiling point. We salt pasta water for flavour, not for faster cooking.

questions.question: What is 'mise en place' in a professional kitchen?

answers.text: Everything prepped and in its place before cooking

questions.fun_fact: French for 'putting in place', it's the discipline of pre-measuring, chopping, and arranging every ingredient so service runs smoothly.

questions.question: Why does cutting onions make you cry?

answers.text: They release a volatile sulphur gas that becomes sulphuric acid in your eyes
Onion juice has a high pH

questions.fun_fact: Crushed onion cells release syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a gas that reacts with the water in your eyes to form a mild sulphuric acid, triggering tears.

questions.question: What happens to an egg's white that makes it firm when cooked?
questions.fun_fact: Heat unfolds the egg's proteins, which then tangle and bond into a solid network — a permanent change called denaturation.

questions.question: 'Confit' traditionally refers to food preserved how?

answers.text: Slowly cooked and stored in its own fat

questions.fun_fact: Confit de canard (duck confit) is a Gascon classic — duck legs cured in salt, then slow-cooked and submerged in their own fat, where they keep for months.

questions.question: Why do chefs rest meat after cooking?

answers.text: It lets muscle fibres relax and reabsorb juices
It lowers the internal temperature for safety

questions.fun_fact: While cooking, juices are pushed toward the centre. Resting redistributes them so they don't all run out when you cut in.

questions.question: Carrots were historically what colour before orange ones were popularised?
questions.fun_fact: Wild carrots were purple, yellow, and white. Orange carrots were cultivated by Dutch growers around the 16th–17th century.

questions.question: Botanically speaking, a banana is classified as a what?
questions.fun_fact: Bananas develop from a single ovary with seeds embedded in the flesh, fitting the botanical definition of a berry. Strawberries, ironically, are not berries.

questions.question: Honey found in ancient Egyptian tombs was reportedly still edible because honey does what?
questions.fun_fact: Honey's low water content, low pH, and natural hydrogen peroxide make it inhospitable to microbes. Sealed properly, it can last thousands of years.

questions.question: Why is chocolate toxic to dogs but not to humans?

answers.text: Dogs are allergic to cocoa butter

questions.fun_fact: Humans metabolise theobromine in hours. Dogs take far longer, letting it build to toxic levels that affect the heart and nervous system.

questions.question: Peanuts are botanically not nuts. What are they?
questions.fun_fact: Peanuts grow underground in pods, like peas and lentils. True nuts, like hazelnuts, grow on trees with a hard shell that doesn't open on its own.

questions.question: Cashews are sold shelled because the shell contains what?

answers.text: An irritant chemical related to poison ivy

questions.fun_fact: Cashew shells contain urushiol, the same skin irritant in poison ivy. Workers handle them carefully, and the nuts are roasted to neutralise residue.

questions.question: Apple seeds contain a compound that releases what in the body when chewed?
questions.fun_fact: Apple seeds contain amygdalin, which releases small amounts of cyanide when chewed. You'd need to eat the seeds from dozens of apples for a harmful dose.

questions.question: Most commercial 'wasabi' served outside Japan is actually made primarily from what?
questions.fun_fact: Real wasabi rhizome is hard to grow and expensive. Most paste worldwide is dyed horseradish with a touch of mustard.

questions.question: Lobsters were historically considered such poor food that in colonial America they were fed mainly to whom?
questions.fun_fact: Lobsters washed up by the thousand and were seen as 'sea cockroaches'. Servants in Massachusetts reportedly had clauses limiting how often they could be fed lobster.

questions.question: Most ground cinnamon sold in North America and Europe is not 'true' cinnamon but which cheaper variety?
questions.fun_fact: Cassia is bolder and cheaper but contains more coumarin, which can be harmful to the liver in very large doses. True 'Ceylon' cinnamon has much less.

questions.question: The Michelin star rating system was originally created to do what?
questions.fun_fact: The Michelin tyre company started the guide in 1900 to encourage motorists to drive more — and wear out more tyres — by giving them places to visit.

questions.question: Which country opened a chain of fake McDonald's-style restaurants, including one called 'Mash Donald's'?
questions.fun_fact: With McDonald's absent from Iran, copycat chains using altered logos and names like 'Mash Donald's' and 'Pizza Hat' have popped up in Tehran.

questions.question: Sushi in pre-modern Japan was originally a method primarily designed to do what?
questions.fun_fact: Early 'narezushi' wrapped fish in fermenting rice for months. The rice was thrown away, and only the preserved fish was eaten. Modern nigiri came later, in Edo Japan.

questions.question: In Japan, slurping noodles loudly at a ramen shop is generally considered what?
questions.fun_fact: Slurping cools noodles, aerates the broth, and signals enjoyment. It's the opposite of Western table manners.

questions.question: What is unusual about how 'fugu' (pufferfish) chefs in Japan are licensed?

answers.text: They train for years to remove organs containing a deadly toxin
They must be born in a coastal prefecture
They can only serve it under government supervision

questions.fun_fact: Pufferfish liver and ovaries contain tetrodotoxin, far deadlier than cyanide. Chefs train for years and must pass a strict exam before they can prepare and serve fugu.

questions.question: In South Korea, what 'dining' activity has become a massive online entertainment genre?

answers.text: Mukbang — eating huge meals on camera

questions.fun_fact: Mukbang ('eating broadcast') hosts livestream themselves eating enormous portions, often earning a living from viewer donations and ads.

questions.question: What is the traditional purpose of tipping the bill in many parts of Japan?

answers.text: There isn't one — tipping is generally not done
To skip the queue next time

questions.fun_fact: In Japan, good service is the standard, not a bonus. Tipping can be seen as awkward or even rude; staff may chase you down to return the money.

questions.question: In Italy, ordering a cappuccino after about 11 a.m. is widely considered what?

answers.text: A foreigner move — locals usually drink it only in the morning

questions.fun_fact: Italians believe milky coffee interferes with digestion after meals, so cappuccino is breakfast-only. Espresso or macchiato is the post-meal norm.

questions.question: In a French restaurant, what does it traditionally mean if you place your knife and fork parallel on your plate?
questions.fun_fact: Crossed cutlery means 'I'm still eating'. Parallel placement, usually at the 4 o'clock position, tells the server they can clear your plate.

questions.question: The world's oldest restaurant still in operation, according to Guinness, is in which city?
questions.fun_fact: Sobrino de Botín in Madrid has been serving roast suckling pig from its wood-fired oven since 1725. The oven has reportedly never been allowed to go out.
